reason: One 48-byte string was sampled during the rounded-fill trace, with no allocating callee resolved below DrawRectangle. This isolated tick does not establish a per-draw cost. Allocation-counter tests measured zero managed bytes across 1,000 warmed solid and rounded fills, including small gradients.

One 48-byte string was sampled with no allocating callee resolved below DrawGlyphRun. This isolated tick does not establish a per-draw cost. A separate allocation-counter test checks warmed repeated glyph draws.
Avalonia's shaping contract returns an owned layout buffer. Each shaping request creates this wrapper; retained glyph runs reuse the result for drawing.
The shaped layout owns a wrapper around pooled glyph storage. The wrapper is created during shaping, while the glyph array is reused from Avalonia's pool.
Avalonia retains the shaped glyph storage through a reference wrapper so layout slices can share its lifetime. This runs during shaping, not each retained draw.
The layout buffer's reference counter releases its pooled glyph storage when the final layout slice is disposed.
Avalonia's ILockedFramebuffer contract returns a disposable lock object. A tile is locked once, while the render thread writes its pixels; drawing a cached tile does not lock it.

SKImage.FromPixels wraps the tile's pixels in a pixmap instead of copying 1 MB per tile. It runs on a tile's first draw after a write; later frames reuse the cached image (DrawOneToOne allocates nothing).
The image that shares the tile's pixels, created on the first draw after a write and cached until the next write.
SkiaSharp registers each new native wrapper in its handle table with a weak reference. One per image snapshot, once per written tile.
SkiaSharp's FromPixels keeps the pixmap alive through a release callback closure. One per image snapshot, once per written tile.
SkiaSharp's handle table entry for a new native wrapper. One per image snapshot, once per written tile.
Assigning a preview sheet changes its image width and height. Avalonia creates property notifications for layout. This runs when a sheet is assigned or recycled.
Assigning a preview sheet changes its caption. Avalonia creates a text property notification. This runs when the caption changes.
Changing the preview view model updates the control's data context. Avalonia creates a property notification for the new context.
ReactiveUI notifies subscribers when the preview view model changes. Each assigned sheet triggers this notification.
Opening document properties creates a file-info object, display strings and property entries in a list. The dialog owns this snapshot.
The properties dialog formats the file size as a display string. Its units array is local to that conversion.
Each metadata value shown by the properties dialog becomes one entry in its snapshot.
Importing a signature copies the source pixels into an owned buffer. It runs when the user imports an image.
A visible signature becomes one immutable image record. Cropping also creates an exact-sized pixel buffer. Full-size images reuse the owned source buffer.
Each submitted print job formats its copy count as text for CUPS. The runtime caches the text of numbers below 300, so only a larger copy count allocates.
Search in Folder keeps each match with its snippet (the result) and lists the file's matches; it runs off the UI thread once per file searched.
The measurement's description is the result shown in the Measure bar and beside the shape; one string per pointer move while measuring.
Reading a drawing's declared scale parses the file's cross-reference data and its viewport and measure dictionaries, once per page when measuring starts on it.
The replacements of the sentence normalizer read their match groups and build the spoken words, once per sentence before it is phonemized; see TextNormalizer.

Normalizing a sentence for the voice rewrites it with generated regular expressions, each replacement making a new string, once per sentence before it is phonemized. Synthesizing the sentence takes hundreds of milliseconds, so this is negligible.

Checking a signature decodes the CMS and builds the certificate chain with System.Security.Cryptography, which allocates, and SignedCms needs the signed bytes as one array. It runs only when the user asks to check signatures.

The page and strip pixel buffers are rented from ArrayPool<byte>.Shared. The pool allocates them the first time a page is recognised (or after it trims idle buffers on a gen 2 GC); later pages reuse them. Seen once per trace.
Finding a language's data builds one path string per folder and language checked, because File.Exists takes a string. It runs once each time Recognise Text is pressed, never per page.
Reading TESSDATA_PREFIX returns a new string. It runs once each time Recognise Text is pressed, never per page.

Checking a downloaded language or voice file reads its size through FileInfo and builds the path of its recorded hash. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed or a download starts, not while reading or rendering.
Listing the language packs still to download builds each pack's path and returns a new list of the missing packs. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed or a download starts.

The download's copy buffer is rented from ArrayPool<byte>.Shared. The pool allocates a buffer when the download continues on a core whose cache is still empty; later downloads on that core reuse it. A download runs only when the person asks for a language.
Starting a language download builds the Refit request and its User-Agent header inside System.Net.Http. It happens once per language downloaded.
Splitting the language setting, for example eng+deu, returns a new list of codes. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed or Preferences opens.

Each recognised word becomes a string (the result), and Tesseract's result iterator is wrapped in one SafeHandle per page. Recognition itself takes hundreds of milliseconds in Tesseract's native code.
The first time a LibraryImport returns a given SafeHandle type, the generated marshaller creates it with new T(), which builds the runtime's per-type activator cache once for the life of the process.

The layout is the result: one immutable object with arrays sized exactly to the pages and rows. It is built only when the zoom, arrangement, rotation or viewport size changes, never while scrolling; lookups on it allocate nothing.

Signing writes a new file: the original bytes plus an incremental update built as text, the cross-reference data it reads (inflated object and cross-reference streams), and a CMS signature from System.Security.Cryptography over the signed bytes, which SignedCms needs as one array. A damaged file also gets its cross-reference entries rebuilt by scanning (PdfRepair) and a full cross-reference stream. It runs once, when the user signs.

Reading layers parses the file's structure and returns new layer records; switching a layer writes a new copy of the file (the original bytes plus a small update with the new default visibility). Both run when the layers panel opens or a box is ticked, never while scrolling.
A layer's visibility is an immutable record, replaced when its box is ticked.

Phonemizing runs once per sentence read aloud, while the previous sentence plays. The phonemes are the returned string, one per sentence. Words are looked up from spans of the text, so a listed word makes no string; a word that needs an ending, a compound or spelling out makes the strings of its derived pronunciation. The token list and the output buffer are reused between sentences and grow only for a longer sentence.
Numbers in a sentence are said as words, for example 1984 as 'nineteen eighty four'; the words are a new string per number, made only for sentences that contain digits.
Preparing a sentence for the voice returns it as a new string with line breaks joined; one per sentence read aloud, built in a stack buffer so the result is the only allocation.

Library code inlined into the speech benchmarks, which the entries for the sentence preparer, the phonemizer, the SSML builder and the PCM converter explain: the returned sentence, phonemes, SSML document or sample array, one per sentence read aloud.
The SSML document sent to Azure for one sentence is the result; one string per sentence, with the text escaped.
The samples are the returned audio for one sentence, handed to the sound output; one array per sentence, sized exactly.

Reading order runs once per page, when the page is first read aloud or shown in Focus Mode, and the result is kept by ReadingDocument. It builds a line object per line of text, a block object per paragraph, the joined text of each block with the page character index of every character (the map that lets the spoken sentence be highlighted on the page), and the lists the XY-cut groups blocks into; all proportional to the page's text.
Flattening a page for Read Aloud returns its text and the matching character map, one string and one int array per page read, sized exactly.

MeloTTS's front end runs once per sentence read aloud, while the previous sentence plays. BERT's cleaning lower-cases and decomposes the sentence into new strings, and the reused cleaning buffer grows once to the longest sentence seen; the piece ids, phones and model input lists are reused between sentences.
The caller's reused list of guessed phones grows once to the longest guess; the phone names themselves are shared strings and the network's state is reused.

Linking replies runs once per save of a document that gained replies: it parses the saved file, gives inline annotations on pages with replies objects of their own, rewrites each reply with its /IRT reference, and returns the file with the update appended as a new array.
The benchmark's local timestamp authority, standing in for a remote one: it builds and signs each token. The app makes none of these allocations; its tokens come from the network.
The document security store is read once when the user checks a document's signatures: the file's structure, the store's certificate streams, and a certificate object for each.
Checking a signature runs when the user asks to see the signatures: it reads the signed bytes, decodes the CMS and any timestamp token, and builds certificate chains.
Signing or timestamping writes a new copy of the file with an incremental update, the CMS signature or token, and its hex form; once per signature.
Field scripts are recognised once, when a form is first edited: the regular expressions' matches, the arguments and field names as strings, and the script record.
Evaluating a calculation reads each field name as a string to look its value up; once per calculated field per edit.
Formatting or reading a number builds the text, with its separators and currency, as new strings; once per field per edit.
Formatting or reading a date converts the field's format into a pattern string; once per date field per edit.
Running a script works on new strings for the value it formats or checks, and a closure for a calculation's field lookups; once per field per edit.
Following a link to another file builds that file's full path, once per click on the link. Nothing here runs while pages draw.
A link written with the other system's folder separators is rewritten once per click so the file can be found; a path that already uses this system's separators is returned as it is.
Closing a tab at a new page records one small entry in the settings; an unchanged newest entry is kept without allocating.
The message about content that cannot be shown is built once per combination of parts and then reused for every document.

The corrections are returned in a new list of five, the list and its array. Copying them into an array of their exact count saved the list but measured 30 to 40 ns slower. Corrections are looked up only when the reader opens the menu on a misspelled word.
Opening the word list file creates its file handle. It happens once per spell checker, when spell checking first starts.

Loading a word list opens its file handle and rents the character, start and hash table arrays from ArrayPool.Shared. The pool allocates them the first time a list is loaded, or after it trims idle buffers on a gen 2 GC; disposing a checker returns them, so a later load reuses them. No string is made per word.

The correction index rents its entry, directory and mark arrays from ArrayPool.Shared the first time a correction is asked for. The pool allocates them the first time (or after it trims idle buffers on a gen 2 GC); disposing the checker returns them, so a later build reuses them.

A correction's string and its cache entry are made the first time that word is offered; offering it again finds it and allocates nothing. Corrections are looked up only when the reader opens the menu on a misspelled word.

A correction's string and its cache entry are made the first time that word is offered; offering it again finds it and allocates nothing. Corrections are looked up only when the reader opens the menu on a misspelled word.

Subsetting builds the new font program the file embeds: the renumbered glyph, metric and cmap tables and the assembled file. It runs when a text box in an installed font is written, once per 128-character block of new letters, never while typing or drawing. SubsetFont measures about 1 ms for a paragraph.
Lists the characters a font maps while its subset's cmap is built, once per subset.

The page and grey buffers are rented from ArrayPool and returned after each read. The trace shows two rents in the whole run, when the pool first fills; every later read reuses them. Detect itself allocates nothing.
Writing a text box makes its /DA, /DS and /RC values once per commit; they are copied into the annotation. Reading a foreign FreeText makes its format once.
The format record kept with a text box: one string per commit, built in a stack buffer.
Reading a text box back to edit it makes the one TextFormat it returns. Settings are parsed into a struct first, so only the final record is allocated.
An installed font's family name read from a text box's record; built-in family names are reused.
A format with values out of range is copied once with usable ones; formats already in range are returned as they are.
Finding an installed face returns a FontMatch describing the face and any synthetic bold or italic, once per commit.

PdfSigner.Sign is inlined into the signing benchmark methods, so its allocations carry their names: the signed copy of the file and its incremental update as strings and bytes, and the CMS signature's ASN.1 reader and writer state. They are the same work the PdfSigner and PdfUpdateWriter entries explain, once per signature, which is a user action.

The benchmark methods open the document inside the measured operation, and the open is inlined into them. The open context holds the open's token, sink and repair log, so each open has its own; it makes its lock and drawing services only when a repair is reported or a page is drawn.

The benchmark methods open the document from a byte array inside the measured operation, and the open is inlined into them. The byte source is the document's handle on those bytes, kept until the document is disposed, one per open.

The object-slot array of a document: one slot for each object number in the cross-reference table, holding the parsed object after its first use. It is made once per open, and again only when authentication or a rebuilt table changes the object count.

The cache of decoded object streams makes its slot arrays when the first stream is cached and doubles them up to the stream limit (128), so a document keeps room for only the streams it has read. Once per document that has object streams.
Opening an FDF file from a byte array wraps the array in the document's byte source, which the object store keeps until it is disposed. One per file read.
A font's code map is made once per font per document: the characters and codes the font shows, in two exact arrays that the form font keeps. The working lists are rented from the array pool.

Opening a document reads its cross-reference table and page tree into an object store, a name table and dictionaries. The import benchmarks include this cost, so it is the baseline to subtract from them. Opening a file is a user action.

Reading an XFDF or FDF file builds the data model: one annotation object per annotation with its text as strings and its numbers as arrays. XFDF goes through XmlReader, which keeps its own node, attribute and name-table state and returns attribute values as strings. FDF goes through the PDF object parser into dictionaries and arrays. Reading a file is a user action, not a render path.

Exporting reads each annotation dictionary into the data model and writes it out. XFDF is written through XmlWriter, which formats attribute values as strings and keeps its own element, namespace and buffer state. FDF is written as PDF syntax straight into a pooled buffer and copied into the result array. Exporting is a user action, not a render path.

Importing reads the file as described for the read benchmarks, then builds one annotation dictionary and object per annotation, queues them per page, links replies and pop-ups, and puts each page's array in place once. It also includes opening the fresh document, which the OpenOnly entry explains. Importing is a user action, not a render path.

Inserting pages is an edit transaction: the transaction and its undo record, the new page set, the copied page dictionaries and the page tree nodes the insertion changes. The carrier objects and their lists are created once per insertion and find nothing to carry in a plain document. Inserting pages is a user action, not a render path.

Everything InsertPlain allocates, plus what the carried structures need: prepared annotation copies, the field nodes and their rebuilt dictionaries, the outline entries and their reserved objects, the named destination and embedded file name entries merged into new name tree leaves, the layer list, and the merged AcroForm, resources and catalog copies. Each is built once per insertion. Inserting pages is a user action, not a render path.

Extracting builds a new document: the builder's object list, the copied page and annotation objects, the same carried structures as InsertBook written into the new catalog, and the file bytes with compressed streams. Extracting pages is a user action, not a render path.

The carriers (forms, outlines, destinations, layers, files, text, context, separations) build their working lists, dictionaries, arrays and reserved objects once per page copy, sized by what the copied pages reference. The separation plan holds one link array per printed page and per-page slots, and is made only when a copied page has a separation dictionary. Copying pages is a user action, not a render path.
The carrier runs once per page copy and creates one object per structure it keeps, with the annotation list of each page and the merged catalog. Copying pages is a user action, not a render path.
Merging into a name tree reads the old entries, sorts old and new together and writes one leaf array, once per tree per page copy.
Comparing the form defaults of two documents builds the font rename table and the renamed default appearance string, once per page copy that carries fields.
Page labels are copied with a style table that keeps pages that shared a style in one run, and written as one number tree, once per page copy.
Copying objects between documents allocates the queue of objects still to copy and the copied dictionaries, arrays and stream data holders, once per object copied.
Writing the whole page tree again, for a delete, a reorder, a direct page edit or an insertion the tree cannot take in place, builds the list of old nodes and the new kids arrays, once per edit.

An in-place insertion or move copies the dictionary and /Kids array of each node on the way down to the position, and of each node a split adds, because stored objects are never changed; that is a few small copies per edit.
Before the first in-place edit of a page set, the check of the tree keeps the set of nodes it has reached, one entry per node, once per page set read.
Committing an edit builds the undo record and the lists of changed objects and trailer entries, once per edit.

Making a page from an image builds the edit's state, the image's pixel buffers and streams, and the page's dictionaries once per image, sized by the image. Making a page is a user action, not a render path.

Inserting pages allocates the carrier, the importer's queue, the reserved ids, the prepared annotation arrays, the page copies and the new page set's entry array, once per insertion. Page editing is a user action, not a render path.
An edit allocates its transaction and the lists that record changed objects and trailer entries, once per edit.
Copying a page dictionary builds its copy once per inserted page.
Reading the source labels of the copied pages builds the label array and a decimal style, once per insertion.
Rebuilding the labels of the new page order builds the label array and a decimal style, once per insertion.
The label ranges are read once after an edit drops the cached ranges.

An uncached separation read makes its working state (entry list, page dictionary, listed-page set and scratch list, findings list) once, and only when a page has a separation dictionary; a document of ordinary pages allocates nothing (ReadOrdinary measures 0 B). The result is cached until an edit (Cached measures 0 B).

Each separation page gets the entry that holds it while grouping, its PdfSeparationPage result record and its colourant name as a string; the page dictionary and entry list grow with the number of separation pages. Once per uncached read.
Each separation page's /Pages array becomes one int array of the page indexes it lists, compared with its group's; the listed-page set grows to the longest array. Once per uncached read.
A Separation or DeviceN colour space gives the result record its colourant names: one string array and one string per colourant. Once per uncached read.
A DeviceN colour space's colourant names become a string array and one string per name for the result record. Once per uncached read.
Grouping makes one build object and member list per printed page, and the list of builds. Once per uncached read.
The result: one PdfSeparationGroup and separation array per printed page, the group array, the findings array and the PdfSeparationInfo record that is cached. Once per uncached read.
The page slots list is built when an edit writes the whole page tree again or recomputes page labels, once per such edit.
Writing the page tree after an edit builds the label list and the tree's working state, once per edit.

Reading the page tree makes one small entry for each leaf page, in an array sized from the root /Count and handed over without a copy; the walk's visited set and ancestor stack are rented. A page that is not encrypted, has plain boxes and no /Kids is recognised from its bytes and parsed only when it is first used. The PdfPage is made on first use. It runs on open, and again after an edit that cannot hand over its pages.

The page set is a snapshot that readers on other threads use, so each page edit that changes the tree in place makes a new set with a copy of the entry array. Its made-page table, link slots and object-number lookup are made only when first asked for, once per page set.
Reading the entries of a name tree builds the entry list once per tree: for a merge, or for the web capture IDS and URLS trees whose content sets the reader returns.
Reading the source's layer state to copy it builds the group list and the sets of hidden and listed groups, once per page copy that reaches a layer.
Extracting pages reserves one object per page and keeps the prepared annotation arrays, once per extraction.
Copying objects into a new document allocates the queue of objects still to copy and the copied dictionaries, arrays and stream data holders, once per object copied.
The builder holds the new document's objects and writes them with compressed streams and a cross-reference table, once per extraction.
A new dictionary's key and value arrays, made for each dictionary a page copy builds; their size follows the entries the copied object holds.
Copying a dictionary for editing (an annotation, a field, the catalog or an outline root) allocates its key and value arrays, once per edited dictionary in a page copy.
A name the target has not seen is added to its name table, once per new name in a page copy.

A PDF text string is decoded to a .NET string: a name tree key or field name compared once per name checked in a page copy, a colourant given as a string once per uncached separation page, or a thread title, URL or content type that a catalog structure read returns to the caller.
The first copy of a page parses the source's objects that were not read yet, so arrays are allocated once per object.
The first copy of a page parses the source's objects that were not read yet, so dictionaries are allocated once per object.

Opening a file creates its byte source once per document: the mapped view and its accessor, or the stream source's 64 KiB page cache. The Memory source reads the whole file into one array by design (File.ReadAllBytes), which is why the Memory rows of the source benchmarks show the file size per open. Opening is a user action.
Opening reads the cross-reference table or streams into one entry array sized to the file's object count, and repair scans a damaged file once. Both run once per open, a user action.

The object store is created once per open with its object slot array, trailer and catalog. ReadStream and RootResolves load an object the first time it is used and keep it in the slot array, so each object is parsed once per document. Edits keep the edited copies until saved. None of this runs when a recorded tile is drawn.

Each document has one name table. It makes its lookup and lock when the first name that is not in the static known-name table is seen, and stores that name's bytes once for every later use in the document.

Parsing an object builds its value: a PdfDictionary or PdfArray allocated once at its final size from the operation-local parse stack, its key and value arrays, and strings with escapes. Parsed objects are cached in the object store, so each is parsed once per document. Inline marked-content property lists are parsed when a page is recorded or its text read, which is once per page; warm tiles replay the recorded picture.
Builds a dictionary that the caller keeps: a parsed object, a clone for an edit, or a generated appearance resource. Runs when an object is first loaded or edited, not when a recorded tile is drawn.
Builds the number array of a generated annotation appearance (its bounding box or matrix). Appearances are generated once per annotation when the page is recorded.

Decode returns a text string as a .NET string and Encode returns the encoded bytes as a new array; both results belong to the caller (titles, outline entries, metadata, annotation text). They run when the caller asks for text, not when a tile is drawn.
The first prefetch of a stream-backed document creates one weak table owned by its object store to remember each dictionary's cache generation. Inlining attributes the table creation to async open.

Catalog reads return records the caller keeps: one thread record and bead array per article thread, one bead per rectangle on the ring, one piece record with its producer name per data dictionary, and the output intent and permission records. A thread read also makes the visited set that stops a broken bead ring. They run when a caller asks for the structure, not when a page renders.

An embedded go-to action read returns records the caller keeps: the action, one target record per step of its path with the step's file name, and the step array. A path with a second step also makes the visited set that stops a looping path. It runs when a caller reads a link or action, not when a page renders.

Action and trigger reads return records the caller keeps: one node per action in a /Next chain with its next array, the typed action record, one trigger with its event name per /AA entry, and the visited set that stops a looping chain. They run when a caller asks for actions, not when a page renders.

Reading /Requirements returns records the caller keeps: one requirement per dictionary with its type spelling, version, penalty and handler list, and the list that holds them. A document with no /Requirements entry returns a shared empty list and allocates nothing; the read runs once when a document opens, not when a page renders.

Checking requirements returns a result record for each requirement, their array and the assessment the caller keeps, with the plain-language messages. A document with no requirements returns a shared empty assessment and allocates nothing; the check runs once when a document opens.

The messages for the user are built once for each unmet requirement and once for the summary, with a builder for the feature list. They are shown in the notice when a document opens and kept in the assessment.

Viewport and measure reads return records the caller keeps: one viewport with its box numbers per /VP entry, one measure with its number format arrays, and for a geospatial measure its point arrays, coordinate system records and names. They run when a caller asks for a page's measures, not when a page renders.
A coordinate system's name is cut from its well-known text as a string the caller keeps, once per coordinate system dictionary read.
Fitting a viewport's world mapping returns one transform record that the caller keeps for the viewport. Converting a point and checking it against the neatline allocate nothing.

Document part and web capture reads return records the caller keeps: one node with its metadata dictionary and child array per document part, one content set with its identifier bytes and sources per web capture set, and the visited sets that stop cyclic part trees and repeated content sets. They run when a caller asks for the structure, not when a page renders.

Document-level reads that return results the caller keeps or the document caches once: Create builds the document and its lazily filled caches, the page set and output intents are read once, and outline, link, URI, info, viewer preference and conformance reads return records and strings. RunContent creates one content interpreter with its graphics state, resource and marked-content stacks per content run, which happens once per text page build or raster scan, and the text page is cached. RunEdit and CurrentSlots copy the page slots for an undoable page edit. None of these run when a recorded tile is drawn.
Spells PDF names and scalar values out as strings that a caller keeps: for the accessibility report, or for the level names and metadata a document part read returns. Both are user actions.

The optional content configuration is read once per document and again when a user chooses another configuration: the group list, the radio button groups, the referenced group numbers, the hidden sets for viewing, printing and exporting, the locked groups, the zoom ranges and limits, the layer order tree and the configuration list. Checking visibility, including at a magnification, reads this snapshot and allocates nothing. Toggling a layer copies the hidden set under the lock and publishes the new set, so render threads read a stable snapshot without locking; a toggle is a user action and costs one small set.

A render cache is created when a document first needs a set of image and drawing settings, then shared by live renderers with those settings. Decode and ToSkImage decode an image and wrap it in a Skia image once per cache; its image limit bounds retained entries. Large pixel arrays are placed on the pinned object heap and become Skia's own pixel memory, so the decode output is not copied.
The image cache's dictionaries are created with each cache for a document's active image and drawing settings.
The colour space, shading, pattern and soft mask caches, created once per document on the first render.
Draw allocates only when the page has no cached picture yet: it records the page and adds its cache entry. Warm tiles take the cached path and allocate nothing, as the warm tile benchmarks measure.

Adds a page's cache entry the first time the page is drawn, evicting the least recently used page beyond the page cap. The first use of a renderer also registers it, weakly, with its document so disposing the document releases the renderer's pictures.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Decoding an image returns its pixels (one gray byte, BGRA or alpha coverage) as a new array the size of the image: the pixels are the result, so there is nothing to pool. Arrays of 64 KiB or more are zeroed arrays on the pinned object heap that Skia then uses as its own pixel memory, so nothing is copied; smaller ones are copied into Skia. A gray image is already kept as one byte per pixel and is not copied again, so a 1536 by 1536 gray image costs 2.3 MiB once, and a scanned page that text recognition renders strip by strip decodes its scan once (8 MiB at 300 dpi) and every strip draws from it. A smaller decode would change the pixels the page shows or recognises, so only the JPEG 2000 and JBIG2 resolution levels are skipped, and only when the page is drawn smaller than the scan. The sample tables of an 8-bit image that /Decode leaves alone are shared; other images build theirs once. Each image is decoded once while it stays in the cache. Small scratch rows use ArrayPool<T>.Shared; arrays of 64 KiB or more use a document-owned or explicitly shared ScratchPools cache with a default 48 MiB retention limit. A first rent of an array size may allocate under this frame.

Reading a JPEG 2000 codestream's main header builds its model: the codestream, image geometry, component list, coding styles, quantization steps and the tile-part list. It is the parsed file, made once per decode, which runs once per image while it stays in the image cache.
A quantization marker is parsed into its step sizes, once for the main header and once for each tile that overrides it. It is part of the parsed header model of one decode.

Opening the tiles of a tile row reads each tile's header into a header state, coding parameters and tables, which are the parsed model of that tile. Tile streams and row sets come from the cache's idle objects, so only the first decode of a cache builds them. It happens once per tile of a decode.

The working objects of JPEG 2000 decodes (the lock, the list of idle code-block decoders, the stack of idle tile streams, and the decoder with its tile row sets) are made when a scratch cache has no idle set. A cache makes as many sets as it has decodes running at the same time, and keeps them for later decodes.
A JPEG 2000 decoder object keeps its list of open tile row sets and its stack of idle ones between decodes; they are made with the decoder, on the first decode of a scratch cache.

A JPEG 2000 decoder keeps its per-component arrays (areas, tile rows, row buffers) between decodes; they are made on the first decode of a scratch cache and again only when a decode has a different number of components.
Opening a decode makes the decoder with its working objects when the scratch cache has none idle; see JpxBlockWorkers.

One JPEG 2000 encode makes its working state once per file: the settings, the marker segments it writes (SIZ, COD, QCD), the tile layout and the tile parameters it resolves the way a decoder reads them, and the small objects that own the pooled stores (the tile encoder, block coder, packet writer, tag trees and their lists). The sample planes, code-block state, coded data and packet buffers rent from one scratch cache shared by all encodes, so they allocate only the first time a size is needed. The file itself is the owned array the caller receives. Folding this state into a reusable encoder object is not possible while the public API takes an image and options per call.

The encoder's lists of small records (tag tree descriptors, packet pieces, packet keys, coded blocks) rent their arrays from the shared scratch cache. The first rent of a size, or a larger tile than any before, allocates the array; later encodes reuse it, which is why the figure is a fraction of an object for each encode.

Each JPEG 2000 decode parses its header model (image geometry, coding styles, quantization, tile parts and tile coding parameters), which is the parsed file and is made once per decode. The decoder, tile streams, component streams, row sources and code-block decoders belong to the scratch cache and are built only when the cache has none idle, so a cache makes as many as it has decodes running at once (and a tiled image uses one stream for each tile column). Arrays of the tile layout rent from the document's scratch pool.

A JPEG decode takes its tables and components (eight Huffman tables, four quantization tables, four components and their arrays) from idle slots and hands them back when it ends. A decode that finds none idle makes a set, so a set is made once for each decode that runs at the same time.

A worker thread's code-block decoder is made when no finished decoder is idle: the first tile of the first decode on a scratch cache makes one for each worker, and later tiles and decodes on that cache reuse them.

The working rows of each tile-component (a strip of code-blocks for every sub-band and a window of rows for every wavelet level) rent as one array from the document's scratch pool. Its size depends on the image width and the code-block height, not on the height of the image. The first decode of a pool, or a decode of an image so wide that the arrays pass the retention limit (48 MiB unless the document sets another), allocates them; every other decode reuses them.

The joined tile data and a decoder's code-block buffers rent from the document's scratch pool; the first rent of a size allocates, and a page larger than the pool's retention limit (48 MiB unless the document sets another) allocates again for the next page.

Encoding several images together returns the globals array and one array per image, which the caller keeps, and holds one rented ink buffer and one components object per image while it matches marks across them. This runs once per document, not per image drawn.

Each JBIG2 encode of a symbol-coded page makes five small owner objects (the runs, the component measures, the components, the symbol matcher and the symbol list), 56 to 76 bytes each, because each owns pooled arrays and must be disposed. Every bitmap, run, hash table and output buffer is rented from the shared array pool; an occasional rent that the pool trimmed shows as a one-off array. An encode runs once per image.

Each JBIG2 decode builds its segment list, region and symbol dictionary settings, symbol stores and arithmetic contexts: a few hundred bytes to a few kilobytes per page decode. Bitmaps are pooled. A decode runs once per image while it stays in the image cache.
The default decode array of an image's colour space, built once per image decode.
A shading or transfer function is parsed into its coefficient arrays once, when the shading is first used, and cached with the shading.
A shading's Skia shader and its colour stops are built once and cached with the shading in the document's render cache.

Loading a font once per font dictionary per document creates its descriptor, program, encoding, widths, glyph text and substitute face. The font retains its selected resource owner for later glyph lookups; the matcher belongs to the drawing service or detached resource owner. One-character texts, predefined CMaps and CID-to-Unicode tables are cached within the selected resource owner; documents using one drawing service share that owner. Generated asset files are shared on disk. Glyph outlines are built on first draw and kept in pages of 256 slots. Warm text tiles, width and text lookups and CMap lookups allocate nothing.

Building a text page creates the page's result: its character array, line and word index arrays, the page text string and segments, and one marks record each time the open marked-content levels change. Text pages are cached per document (16 pages, least recently used first), and warm find and hit test allocate nothing.

Structure reads return their results: the structure tree's elements and kids, the role map chain, the marked-content recording of a page (glyphs, text and bounds per MCID), tagged nodes, and the inferred layout's paragraph and heading nodes with their text and item indexes. They run when a reader asks for structure, once per page or document, not when a tile is drawn.

The accessibility report is a user action that returns a report: one page record per page, one finding per problem with its message, counts, the structure scan's element map and visited set, and page classification strings.

Saving a document that claims PDF/A reopens the written file to check it against the claimed level: a copy of the output, the reopened document, its validation report and the claim check returned to the caller. When the file breaks the level, the repair converts it and returns the repaired file. Saves of unclaimed documents skip this.
A PDF/A conversion opens its working copy as a new document, and the first text it reads creates that document's font matcher and its substitute face cache, once per document.

PDF/A validation is a user action that returns a report with one result per rule of the level. Each run builds its walk state (visited-object sets, font, colour space and glyph caches, operand stacks, the XMP tree and cross-reference sections) and the rule lists, then releases them. Validation never runs while rendering.

The conformance report is a user action that returns a report: the PDF/A claim, the output intents and one observation per feature, with the lists of fonts, forms, images, graphics states and patterns that page content uses, each collected once.

The content usage walk serves two user actions, optimising and the conformance report. It records, per resource dictionary, the names page, form, pattern and appearance content uses, plus the fonts and images drawn, as sets built once per run. Neither action runs while viewing or rendering.
The raster report returns one page record per page and one image record per scanned image with its filter names. It is a user action that walks the whole document once.

The annotation data model is what a read returns and a write takes: one annotation object per annotation with its text as strings and its numbers as arrays. A read keeps the XML or object tree it parses only while parsing; the FDF write goes straight into a pooled buffer and the XFDF write into a rented stream, so only the result array is new. These are user actions, not a render path.

Each save walks the page tree once to find trap network annotations: the walk's state, its stack of /Kids cursors and the set of page tree nodes seen, which ends a looped tree. Pages are not added to the set, so a flat tree keeps it to the root. A page with a trap network adds one page record and the list that holds it.
Checking a trap network collects the object numbers of its page's content streams, resources and form resources into two sets, once per page that has a network. Pages without one are not walked.

Checking a /Version network builds the set of object numbers its array lists, sized to the array, once per page with a network. A /LastModified network compares its page's appearance states in two lists only when an edit touched the page's annotations.
Removing or moving a trap network builds the page's new /Annots array, once per changed page.
Removing or fixing a trap network records the page's or array's previous state in the open edit so the change can be undone, and copies the page when its /Annots is direct; once per changed page.
A save that finds a trap network takes the set of edited object numbers once, to tell which networks an edit touched.
Taking the edited object numbers copies them into one sorted array per call. A save calls it once, and only when it finds a trap network.

A save that finds a trap network keeps one check result per network and the set of edited object numbers, inlined from its callees. When a network must change, it opens one undoable edit and returns one change record per page in the save report.

Each operation creates the save report it passes to the check; ValidateNetwork and RemoveStaleNetwork also hold the page description, its sets and the edit set inlined from the library. These are the allocations the trap network entries above explain.
Editing annotations creates the new annotation dictionaries, their text, date and colour values and the page's new /Annots array. Editing is a user action.
A page edit rewrites the page tree: it collects the nodes, copies inherited attributes into moved pages and writes new Kids arrays, all inside one undoable transaction. Editing is a user action.
Writing an OCR text layer adds new content streams and wraps the page's contents in a new array. It is a user action.

Optimising is a user action that rewrites the whole file once. Each run opens a working copy, so every object is parsed again (OptimizerGraph.Visit inlines those loads) and the reachable-object graph, renumbering map and cross-reference rows are built at the file's size. Duplicate finding keeps one content hash per stream; font subsetting runs each page's content once to collect glyphs and builds the subset font's tables and file as new arrays; image recoding produces the new JPEG or bilevel data; the writer compresses object streams with one ZLib encoder each; the report lists every action and skip. None of it runs while viewing or rendering.

Reading an XMP packet goes through a forward-only XmlReader, which keeps its own node, namespace and name-table state and returns element text as strings. The optimiser reads the packet once per run to keep or update document metadata; viewers read it once per document.

Saving collects the reachable objects, writes the cross-reference rows, computes the file ID and compresses streams with one ZLib encoder per stream. The saved bytes are returned to the caller. Saving is a user action.
Opening a document through the adapter creates the library document and its wrapper. Opening is a user action.

The adapter converts library results into the app's records: the wrapper's state on open, outline items, links and viewer rectangles. RenderNative creates the document's renderer entry on the first render; later tiles find it and allocate nothing, as the warm tile benchmarks measure.
The adapter's annotation editor: its name table, the new markup's dictionaries and the text layer's font list. Annotation and text layer edits are user actions.
The annotation name index, created once per annotation editor.
The tagged block walker and character map build the reading order blocks the app asks for, once per page.

Library code inlined into a HyperPDF benchmark method allocates under the benchmark's name. Each such site is the same first-use or result work the library entries explain: opening documents and creating renderers in cold benchmarks, decoder state in the codec benchmarks, the returned encoded bytes, image, report or page records, and the copied hidden set of a layer toggle. Every warm render, text query, font lookup, colour and syntax benchmark measures zero.
Library code inlined into the accessibility report benchmark: opening the document and the report's result records, as the accessibility entry explains.
Mapping the app's settings to the library's options and the library's report to the app's creates the option record, the report record and its lists. Once per run, when the user clicks Save a Copy.

Taking the snapshot lists the pages that hold annotations removed but kept, so they can be left out of the copy and put back. Once per run, only when such annotations exist; a document without them allocates nothing.

A page whose annotation array still holds a removed annotation gets a copy of the array without it for the length of the save, which the writer then writes. Once per such page per save; a page without a removed annotation in its array is skipped after a scan and allocates nothing.

Exporting or printing pages composes a new document: the builder with its object tables and name table, and the importers that copy each page. The new document is the result. It is built once per export, which the user asks for.
Laying pages on sheets adds each sheet's page dictionary, content and resources to the new document being exported, once per sheet, when the user prints or exports pages.

A page edit opens an undo transaction in the document's history, with the lists of object states and trailer entries it records so the edit can be undone, and the set of pages it touches. Once per page edit, which the user asks for.

After a page edit the published page sizes are replaced by a new array when a size changed; published arrays are never written to, so readers see one whole array. Once per page edit that changes a size.

The page size array is the document's published state: readers hold it without a lock, so an edit that changes the page count or a size publishes a new array and never writes into an old one. Once per such page edit; an edit that changes nothing keeps the array.

Reading a tagged page builds the structure reader's node tree (a node, its child list and its glyph index array per structure element and marked content id), the reader's builder, object resolver and used-id set, and the blocks returned with their character index arrays. The text of a node is only read when asked, so the walk reads none. The block walker and its index buffers are reused by the thread. Once per page, which the reading order keeps.
A page's characters are the result, copied once into the caller's list; the reading order keeps them, so this runs once per page.

Writing the first text layer on a document creates its annotation editor state: the font and shaper caches and the layout and name tables it picks fonts with. The layer's fonts and the font list are made for each page written. Text recognition runs when the user asks, once per page.

Writing a recognised page's text layer creates the document's annotation editor state the first time, and the layer's font list for each page written; see HyperPdfDocumentTextLayers.AddTextLayer. Text recognition runs when the user asks, once per page.
The text layer's font list holds the built in font's dictionaries and the list of fonts handed to the writer. Made for each page a text layer is written to.

Writing a text layer puts the built in font's wrapper and its font dictionary into the page's new resources. They are objects of the edited page, made once for each page written. A list of one font, the word names and the use flags stay on the stack.

The document's annotation editor object and its lock are made the first time an annotation edit or a text layer asks for them. The page caches, name index, text layout and font state are made only when an edit first needs each one.
A document creates the service for a feature the first time it is asked for it, and keeps the table of services; later asks return the same one.
The first request for any feature of a document creates the document's table of feature services; later requests find it.

Starting a download builds the request, its response and the part file's stream inside System.Net.Http and System.IO, and the part file's path. It happens once per downloaded file, when the person asks for a language or voice.
Benchmark harness code: the output stream that stops the run at its first write, and the mapping calls the benchmark makes on purpose. Not shipped.

Library code inlined into the recognise-and-write benchmark: the renderer state that draws the scanned page for recognition, and the text layer writer's state, which the page rendering and text layer entries explain. One page per operation.

Library code inlined into the language check: the codes parsed from the setting, each pack's file size read through FileInfo, and the list of missing packs, as the OCR language entries explain. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed.
The measurement's description is the result shown in the Measure bar and beside the shape; one string per pointer move while measuring.
The records the benchmarks build on purpose: a remembered tab, and the signature image made from imported pixels (see the signature image entries).
The drawn mark is the result: its coordinate and stroke length arrays, made once per stroke drawn on the signature pad.
The baseline that uses SkiaSharp's array API on purpose: arrays of colours and offsets, and the shader object, which SpanStops is measured against.
Subscribing allocates the subscription and its wrappers inside ReactiveUI.Primitives, and creating the read-only view allocates the view; both are what the benchmark compares.
The benchmark creates a spell checker for every operation to measure loading a word list; the checker object is created once per word list.
ColdOpenAndRender and FirstRecordOnOpenDocument create a renderer for every operation, which turns its render options' list of hidden colorants, an ImmutableArray, into the key of its cache.
ColdOpenAndRender opens a new document on every operation, and a document makes its table of renderer caches, one per set of render options, when its first renderer is made.
ColdOpenAndRender opens a new document on every operation, and a document makes its table of renderer caches, one per set of render options, when its first renderer is made.
ColdOpenAndRender opens a new document on every operation, and a document makes its table of renderer caches, one per set of render options, when its first renderer is made.
Each asynchronous read waits with Task.Delay, which creates a timer, its promise and the cancellation registration. That wait is the simulated slow device the benchmark is run against. Not shipped.
One 64-byte context per open holds the cancellation token, recovery switches and the repair log, so a document can say whether it was repaired. Opening is a user action, not a render path.
The repair log is created on the first report only, so a clean open allocates none of it. A damaged open allocates the log list, its de-duplication set and their backing arrays once.
The de-duplication set of the repair log, created with the log on the first report of a damaged open.
The backing array of the repair log's de-duplication set, created on the first report of a damaged open.

The parsed notices are the result the Licences window keeps: for each of the 70 or so components, its licence text as one string, its name and field strings, its entry, and the group lists. The file is decoded into a rented buffer, not a string, and lines are read from that buffer. It runs once, when the user opens the Licences window, and is not a render path.

The reader fills the entry and group lists the document keeps, one list for each licence group. Licence text is collected in a rented buffer, so each text becomes one string. It runs once, when the user opens the Licences window, and is not a render path.

Reads one bundled substitute face the first time a document needs it: the resource stream and its name, a byte array of the face's CFF data (about 15 to 30 KB, kept by the parsed program for its lifetime), the CffProgram, the glyph source and the face object. The face is cached for the process, so this happens at most once per face and never while rendering.
Parsing a bundled face builds its charset, encoding and private dictionary tables once, when the face is first read. The program is cached for the process and never rebuilt while rendering.

Reading a page builds the object model the editor works on: one object per painted operation, a glyph array and a Unicode string for each text object, path segments, marks and the clip chain, and the parser's own state stack. Writing it again builds one byte array per text show so the TJ array can be rewritten and, in Preserve mode, one output buffer. Page object parsing and regeneration are editing actions that run once per edit. The render hot path does not call them.

Applying a redaction opens a working copy, reads each marked page into objects, rewrites the content, blanks image pixels, rewrites the ToUnicode maps, prunes resources, scrubs metadata and builds the overlay. Each step allocates its model, its decoded buffers and its rewritten streams. Applying is a user action that ends in a save. The render hot path does not call it.
Inlined library calls carry the benchmark's name: opening the document, applying the redaction and writing the saved copy to the output stream. The pages and the picture are built once in setup.
Inlined library calls carry the benchmark's name: the byte array a regenerate returns, and the objects an edit benchmark parses before it changes them.

Async load-ahead of a stream or file source. When a read really waits, the compiler's state machine is boxed once and a continuation is queued; a source whose pages are cached, and every mapped or in-memory source, completes without either.
One async read of a run of cache pages: a pooled run buffer (rented, returned in the same call) and the state machine box and continuation of the awaited read.
The awaited read of the file or stream: the box of the framework's own async read and the continuation that resumes after it.
Waiting for the stream's turn when another async load holds it; allocates only on contention.

A walk that loads a page's objects ahead of use: the walk's sets and lists, the merged range list and the walk's state machine. Made once per page and cache generation, then skipped while nothing is evicted; the per-dictionary mark is a one-off entry in a ConditionalWeakTable.

Cold async opening walks the page-tree references once per source and cache generation. The walk allocates visited sets, frontier lists and sorted byte ranges. On the 928-page source benchmark the largest sampled groups were about 44 KB of hash entries, 24 KB of object IDs and 30 KB of ranges per open. They are not part of warm page or tile replay.

The compiler-generated async prefetch methods allocate a state-machine box and continuations when file reads suspend. The walk also creates its frontier once per cold open. Warm prefetch hits return a completed ValueTask without these objects.
The prefetch mark is created once for each page or tree dictionary when async load-ahead first visits it; a cached generation reuses the mark.

Cold async prefetch sorts cross-reference offsets to estimate object byte extents. The 928-page benchmark allocated an approximately 258 KB long array and one list per open. It is built once for the source and is not used in warm replay.

On .NET 10 the Flate decoder uses a ZLibStream, DeflateStream, inflater and tracking wrapper for each decoded compressed stream. The 928-page cold-open benchmark decodes two such streams per open. The .NET 11 span decoder does not create these wrappers.
Opening with a cancellable token: the options copy that carries the token, plus the state machine box and continuations of the awaited loads. One set per open.
The async search walk: the iterator's state machine, the reused match list, and one match array for each page that has a match.
The async text walk: the iterator's state machine, once per walk.
Async form whose load-ahead really waited: the state machine box and continuation. Skipped, with no allocation, once the page is loaded; the allocation test checks that.
Slow path of GetPageAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of GetTextPageAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of GetOutlineAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of GetLinksAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of ScanAnnotationsAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Async save: the state machine box and continuation of the awaited copy and write, one set per save.
Slow path of RenderAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Async render whose load-ahead really waited: the slow path's state machine box and continuation. The fast path allocates nothing; the allocation test checks that.
The sorted object offsets used to find the bytes an object spans, built once per store on the first load-ahead of an object graph.
The benchmark harness: the opened-document wrapper, the delegates and tasks that start parallel renders, the task array and the throttled streams. Not library allocations.
Caching a freshly decoded image, once per image while it stays in the 64 MiB image cache: its map entry and the growth of the map. Never runs when a recorded tile is drawn.
The per-entry lock of a freshly decoded image, once per image while it stays in the image cache.

The record of one image decode in progress, made once per image that is not cached so a second thread waits for it instead of decoding again. A thread that waits for another thread's decode adds the monitor state it sleeps on; the task for async waiters exists only when one waits. Never runs for a cached image or when a recorded tile is drawn.
The list of images a page's picture drew, published once per recorded picture so renders can read it without a lock.

Adding up the picture cache's memory counts each shared image once, using a scratch set that grows to the number of distinct images. It runs only after a render recorded a picture, never when a recorded tile is drawn.

An object stream (or cross-reference stream) is decoded into one exact-size array. The store keeps only the last 8 decoded object streams within 4 MiB, so a stream that was evicted is decoded again the next time one of its unparsed objects is read. Each object is still parsed once per document, so this is a first-read cost, not a render cost.

Reading an object stream's header builds its object-number and offset arrays and the index that holds them next to the decoded data. It runs once per decode of an object stream, which is again after the bounded cache evicted it, and never when a recorded tile is drawn.
One 64-byte context per open holds the cancellation token, the recovery switches and the repair log, so a document can report whether it was repaired. Opening is a user action, not a render path.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates the border of a link annotation that has no appearance and names a border: its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per such link when the page's annotations are recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates the caret symbol of a caret annotation that has no appearance: its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per caret when the page's annotations are recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates the outline preview of a redaction annotation that has no appearance: its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page's annotations are recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.
Importing a field value is an edit: it creates the edit scope that holds the field's copy before it changes. This runs once per imported field, never while rendering.

Importing a field value redraws the field's appearance stream, which allocates its dictionaries, arrays and edit-layer entries. This runs once per imported field; warm rendering draws the stored appearance.
Writing a text value encodes the string and the arrays that hold it. This runs once per imported field.
Redrawing a field's appearance reads the field's font once to map characters to codes. This runs when a field is edited or imported, never while rendering.
Reading a field for an edit describes its widget and font size. This runs once per edited or imported field.
Adding a new object to the store, such as a redrawn appearance stream, grows the store's tables. This runs once per edit.
Importing form data opens one undoable edit that records each object's previous state so Undo can put it back. This runs once per user-approved import.

Painting a path creates the Skia path and the objects SkiaSharp registers for its handle. This happens once per painted path while a page or its annotations are recorded; warm tiles replay the picture.

Painting a path creates the Skia path and the objects SkiaSharp registers for its handle. This happens once per painted path while a page or its annotations are recorded; warm tiles replay the picture.

Stroking a path creates the Skia path and the objects SkiaSharp registers for its handle. This happens once per stroked path while a page or its annotations are recorded; warm tiles replay the picture.

Regenerating a form appearance writes its retained content bytes, form stream, bounding box, matrix and resource dictionaries. Compression creates encoder state. This is an edit operation; warm rendering draws the recorded appearance.

The first edit of a field in a multi-byte font reads every code its CMap defines, one-byte and two-byte, and turns them around into a table from character to code. That table is built once per font per document and cached with the document's fonts; later edits of any field in that font only look characters up. It is dropped when the fonts are cleared. Warm rendering never builds it.

Storing a regenerated appearance records the widget's edit copy and adds the new appearance object to the document's edit table, which grows its arrays and buckets now and then. This is an edit operation.

Regenerating a push button resolves its caption font, encodes the caption, lays out the icon and caption and writes the new appearance: font and icon lists, caption bytes and operand strings. This is an edit operation; warm rendering draws the recorded appearance.

Drawing a beveled or inset border builds the corner lists of the lit and shaded sides as small arrays while the appearance is generated. This is an edit operation; warm rendering draws the recorded appearance.

Regenerating a rich text field reads its XHTML value with a forward-only XmlReader, which allocates its reader, name table, node and namespace state, and then lays out each paragraph: encoded codes, unit arrays, line lists and the colour and content bytes of the new appearance. This is an edit operation; warm rendering draws the recorded appearance.

Reading rich text builds its paragraphs: styles for each element, runs, collapsed text and the stack of open styles. Writing a rich value builds the XHTML with a forward-only XmlWriter. These run when a rich field is edited or its appearance is regenerated, never when a warmed tile is drawn.
Reading a CSS style attribute creates the style records for each declaration it applies. This runs while rich text is read for an edit, never when a warmed tile is drawn.

Laying out a rich text paragraph flattens its runs into unit arrays and breaks them into lines. These arrays and line lists support the new appearance and are dropped afterwards. This is an edit operation.
Choosing the font of a rich text run adds the font to the list of fonts the appearance uses. This is an edit operation.

Reading a widget's default appearance parses its /DA string into a font name, size and colour record. This runs while an appearance is generated for an edit or a regenerated widget, never when a warmed tile is drawn.
Storing a regenerated appearance adds an object to the document's edit table, which grows its bucket array now and then. This is an edit operation.

Regenerating text and choice appearances formats content operands and font names, splits multiline text into line records and writes the new appearance. These strings, line arrays and scratch lists occur during edits, never when a warmed tile is drawn.
Generating a button mark creates its appearance operands and glyph bytes before the result is saved in the widget's appearance stream. This runs during filling or regeneration, not warm rendering.
A form edit parses the field's default-appearance string into a font, size and colour record. Decoding names and formatting stroke colours creates strings and builder buffers for the new appearance.

Form appearance generation resolves the selected font and encoding, splits supplied text into Unicode runes, and creates encoded glyph bytes and width arrays. The resulting codes feed the new appearance; warm rendering does not run this editor path.
Resolving a field for an edit collects its widget controls into a list of control records, including direct controls and referenced widgets.

An undoable form edit clones changed dictionaries and collects original-to-copy mappings. Committing enumerates those copies and writes their replacement objects, preserving the original revision for undo.

Regenerating widgets creates one form-edit transaction and the rewritten appearance data for each resolved control. These objects support the edit and undo; the warmed render path uses cached pictures.
Resolving a form field for reading or filling creates its inherited attributes, control list and resolved widget record. Form inspection and editing run outside warmed rendering.
Filling a checkbox creates an undoable form edit and rewrites its checked state and appearance references.
A checkbox without an on-state appearance gets a new appearance dictionary and generated mark stream when it is filled.
Writing a button value creates the PDF value and state names stored in its field and widget dictionaries during filling.
Reading calculation order tracks visited field names in a hash set to omit duplicates. The set and its entry and index arrays are scratch for this form-order query.
Reading tab order collects widget sort keys in a list and its backing array, then appends their indexes to the caller's output. These keys preserve row, column or structure order during the query.

Resetting a field creates a form-edit builder, its replacement dictionary mappings and cloned field or widget dictionaries. The builder commits the default value and regenerated appearances as one field update.
Regenerating widgets creates one form-edit builder and the rewritten appearance data for each resolved control. These objects support the edit; warmed rendering uses cached pictures.
Resolving a form field for reading or filling creates its inherited attributes, control list and resolved widget record. Form inspection and editing run outside warmed rendering.
Filling a checkbox creates a form-edit builder and rewrites its checked state and appearance references.
A checkbox without an on-state appearance gets a new appearance dictionary and generated mark stream when it is filled.
Writing a button value creates the PDF value and state names stored in its field and widget dictionaries during filling.
Reading calculation order tracks visited field names in a hash set to omit duplicates. The set and its entry and index arrays are scratch for this form-order query.
Reading tab order collects widget sort keys in a list and its backing array, then appends their indexes to the caller's output. These keys preserve row, column or structure order during the query.

Resetting a field creates a form-edit builder, its replacement dictionary mappings and cloned field or widget dictionaries. The builder commits the default value and regenerated appearances as one field update.
Resolving form field flags reads the field type spelling into a string for edit dispatch.

Creating the render surface wraps Skia handles. SkiaSharp creates lock and bookkeeping objects for each handle it registers. The surface is created once per renderer, which is once per document in this benchmark.
The render surface holds one reusable pixel description, created with the surface. It is created once per renderer, which is once per document in this benchmark.
The render surface holds one reusable empty bitmap that borrows each target's pixels, created with the surface. It is created once per graphics thread and backend.
The render surface holds one reusable canvas wrapper that is pointed at each target in turn, created with the surface. It is created once per graphics thread and backend.
The grayscale paint is made the first time a grayscale page is drawn on a graphics thread; colour pages never make it. It is made once per graphics thread and backend.
The grayscale paint carries one colour-matrix filter, made with the paint the first time a grayscale page is drawn on a graphics thread.
SkiaSharp tracks each native handle it wraps with a weak reference. The surface wraps a few handles when it is created, once per graphics thread and backend.
SkiaSharp creates a lock object for the canvas wrapper it registers. The wrapper is made once with the render surface, per graphics thread and backend, and then reused for every target.

The first page drawn on a graphics thread creates that thread's render surface, whose constructor the JIT inlined into DrawPage: one reusable empty bitmap that borrows each target's pixels. It is made once per graphics thread and backend; later pages reuse it.

The first page drawn on a graphics thread creates that thread's render surface, whose constructor the JIT inlined into DrawPage: one reusable pixel description. It is made once per graphics thread and backend; later pages reuse it.

The first page drawn on a graphics thread creates that thread's render surface, whose constructor the JIT inlined into DrawPage: one reusable canvas wrapper. It is made once per graphics thread and backend; later pages reuse it.

SkiaSharp creates a lock object for each native wrapper it registers. The first page drawn on a graphics thread makes the render surface's wrappers, whose constructor the JIT inlined into DrawPage; later pages reuse them.

A document makes its pattern paint cache (the cache object, its lock and its map) when a page first selects a pattern. The map is the cache's result, so it is made once per document and render settings.
The pattern paint cache's map grows as paints for new placements of a pattern are added. A page that selects the same pattern at the same place again allocates nothing.
The pattern paint cache's map makes its bucket array when the first paint is added and grows it with the paints. A page that selects the same pattern at the same place again allocates nothing.
A document makes its pattern paint cache when a page first selects a pattern; it is shared by every later page of the document and render settings.
The pattern paint cache makes its lock when a document first selects a pattern; it is shared by every later page of the document and render settings.

The first decode of a document adds its stream to the in-progress table, and publishing the image adds it to the image map, which is the cache's result. The first insertion into each makes its entry array, and the map grows with the images cached.

The first decode of a document adds its stream to the in-progress table, and publishing the image adds it to the image map, which is the cache's result. The first insertion into each makes its bucket array, and the map grows with the images cached.
